findings.title: Exact integrating-factor AB3: decay factors on the history tendencies — removes the measured first-order split error at ~zero cost
findings.what: Production computes theta' = decay*(theta + b0*T_n + b1*T_{n-1} + b2*T_{n-2}) — the whole AB3 increment is damped once, a Lie split that MATH_energy.md eq. 32 shows is a tendency deficit -(z/2)*dt*T per step (z = lambda*dt), and which P5 measured as THE dominant dt error (D80/D30 = -1.42..-1.51, theory -1.50 for pure first order). The exact IF-AB3 (AB3 applied to e^{lambda t}*theta, the standard scheme in pseudo-spectral turbulence DNS) is theta' = d*(theta + b0*T_n + b1*d*T_{n-1} + b2*d^2*T_{n-2}), d = decay. Its constant-T increment factor is e^{-z}(23/12 - 16/12 e^{-z} + 5/12 e^{-2z}) = 1 - z/2 + z^2/6 + O(z^3) = phi_1(z) + O(z^3) (my expansion; phi_1 = exact), so the -(z/2) deficit cancels through O(z^2): the first-order dt term is gone, and so is the -1.09e-5 SPE / -5.8e-7 VIE budget residual r_IF of Part XIV. Stability on the imaginary axis (advection) is unchanged (lambda=0 modes see plain AB3); the decay factors only shrink. Implementation: in lean32ek_fast, e = 1-d is already an operand of the same step; d*T = T - e*T and d^2*T = apply it twice keep the expm1 precision trick; d^2 lives in registers.

findings.title: ETD3-AB (phi-function multistep) as the exact fallback to IF-AB3; one-step ETDRK4 not worth it here
findings.what: Cox-Matthews-style multistep ETD replaces TS-2's decay powers with per-mode coefficient tables b_j(z) built from phi functions: exact for constant T, where IF-AB3 is exact only to O(z^3) — a relative ~ z^3 ~ 7e-9 residual at the most-damped mode, negligible. Community precedent for exponential SQG stepping: GeophysicalFlows.jl's decaying-SQG example uses stepper="FilteredETDRK4", dt=0.03, n=256, nu=1e-19, n_nu=4 (module default is RK4). But one-step ETDRK4 costs 4 RHS evals/step with per-eval imaginary-axis stability 2sqrt(2)/4 = 0.707 <= AB3's 0.724, and our linear part is 293x below even AB3's real-axis limit (MATH_energy Part 2c) — ETD's stiff-regime advantage never engages. Conclusion: prefer IF-AB3 (TS-2); keep ETD3-AB only if TS-2's gate run surprises.

dead_ends.idea: Stability-optimal explicit RK (Kinnmark-Gray): 3rd-order K-stage schemes with hyperbolic stability sqrt((K-1)^2-1)
dead_ends.why_not: Per-RHS-eval imaginary stability is sqrt((K-1)^2-1)/K = 0.775 (K=5) / 0.845 (K=7) vs AB3's 0.724 — at most ~17% fewer evals at the stability bound. But accuracy binds first: AB3's h^3 error only reaches production's current dt error near h ~ 1.4e-5 (n ~ 14, ladder bound), where AB3 needs 1 RHS eval/step vs KG's 5-7. Per frame: AB3+IF at n=28 = 28 evals; KG7 even at n=14 = 98 evals; each eval is ~2.3 ms of the 2.698 ms f32 step, so KG is a 3-5x loss. Sources: Kinnmark & Gray 1984, Math. Comput. Simul. 26(2) 87-92 and 26(3) 181-188; Vogl et al. 2019 (doi 10.1029/2019MS001700) use the 5-stage variant where stability (not accuracy) binds — not our regime. Read: abstracts/search summaries.

dead_ends.idea: ETDRK4 / IF-RK4 one-step exponential schemes as the production stepper
dead_ends.why_not: 4 RHS evals/step at per-eval imaginary stability 2sqrt(2)/4 = 0.707 <= AB3's 0.724; the stiff-linear advantage never engages (lambda_max*dt = 1.9e-3, 293x below AB3's real-axis limit, MATH_energy Part 2c). ~9.5 ms/step f32 for no larger stable dt. Covered as the negative half of TS-6.

dead_ends.idea: AB4 (higher-order multistep)
dead_ends.why_not: Imaginary stability ordinate ~0.43 < AB3's 0.72 (Ghrist-Fornberg-Reeger, read: abstract) — smaller stable dt — plus a fourth stored tendency (+67 MB complex64 read/write per step). Worse on both axes for an advection-limited problem.

dead_ends.idea: Leapfrog with Robert-Asselin(-Williams) filter
dead_ends.why_not: ISB 1.0 per eval (1.38x AB3) looks attractive, but the RA/RAW filter degrades amplitude accuracy below AB3's 3rd order and adds artificial damping of exactly the kind the bias gates catch (the project's dominant measured error is already a tiny systematic damping deficit); max gain bounded by the same CFL margin (n=28 -> ~n=20, 1.4x) while replacing a bitwise-validated AB3 pipeline. Risk/benefit worse than TS-3.

dead_ends.idea: Parareal / PFASST / MGRIT parallel-in-time
dead_ends.why_not: Published evidence is negative for advection-dominated and chaotic problems: Parareal is not unconditionally stable for hyperbolic equations (Bal, stat.uchicago.edu/~guillaumebal/PAPERS/StabPararealPDE.pdf); high-wavenumber instability (Ruprecht, 'Wave propagation characteristics of Parareal'); convergence worsens as viscosity drops and with larger Lyapunov exponents; even with remedies speedups ~2-6 at large extra GPU cost (parallel-in-time.org survey). Read: abstracts. And the workload is already embarrassingly parallel over ensemble members, where extra GPUs buy throughput at efficiency 1.0 — PinT's <<1.0 efficiency cannot win.

dead_ends.idea: Richardson extrapolation across two dt runs to cancel the first-order split term
dead_ends.why_not: ~1.5-2x the solver work per frame to remove an error that TS-2 removes for free inside one run.

dead_ends.why_not: Interpolated frames change what a training sample IS (no longer a solver state on the fixed 2e-4 grid) — science change. TS-4's integer-n adaptivity gets the same gain without touching frame semantics.

findings.title: Compact kept-mode (2/3-rule block) storage of state, compensation, and AB3 history — bitwise
findings.what: Store theta hi, lo, T_-1, T_-2 (and edec, kinv) only on the kept square block rows [0,1366)+[2731,4096) x cols [0,1366) = 2731x1366 = 44.5% of the 4096x2049 half-plane (29.8 MB vs 67.1 MB per c64 field). The AB3+tendency+compensated-update fusion reads uqh/vqh via a two-span gather of the full RFFT outputs (contiguous 10.9 KB row chunks, coalesced); hi is written back full-shape (zeros outside the block) so the theta C2R input is unchanged and no extra pad kernel or defensive-copy change is needed. Bitwise because edec = 1 outside KMAX makes the update exactly zero there: in compensated_update, u = a - 1*a = 0 and lo' = r2 + (r - 1*r) = 0 in floating point, and kept-mode values depend only on kept-mode operands (elementwise); the forcing patches (8x8 corners) lie inside the block. Tendencies outside the block only ever feed modes the damping zeroes, so truncating them changes nothing observable.

findings.title: Transposed spectral layout + pruned per-axis FORWARD transforms and pruned C2C first pass (inverse side excluded)
findings.what: Keep all spectral arrays transposed (kx-major) and compact (XR-1). Forward products: rfft(uq, axis=-1) (row R2C, unchanged 98 us) -> slice kx[0:1366] fused into one transpose (2x44.8 MB) -> batched 1-D C2C over the trailing 4096 axis on 1366 rows. This replaces cuFFT's 41%-efficiency 2049-wide strided column pass with a slice-transpose + a 78-86%-efficiency contiguous row pass over only kept columns. The (u - i v) C2C becomes: build_w_T writes only the 2731 nonzero-kx rows (89.5 MB, not 134.2), ky row pass on 2731 of 4096 batches, one transpose+pad, full kx row pass. The theta IRFFT stays a single fused C2R (see dead ends): only its input pad comes from the compact state. The leftover 1/4096 normalizations fold into the products fusion as exact power-of-two multiplies (bitwise-neutral), and ifft-over-ky is done as conj(fft(conj(.))) to avoid XLA's per-call DoBlasScal.

evidence.source: Part X kernel table: half-plane column pass 40-41% peak (42% excessive sectors), full-plane C2C column pass 51% (bank conflicts); row passes/products 78-88%

findings.title: JAX/jaxlib 0.4.28 -> 0.11.2+/0.12 stack evaluation: new MLIR fusion emitters are the only solver-relevant gain; C2R copy+scal persist; cuDNN break with torch 2.3.1
findings.what: Facts established from primary sources: (1) XLA's new MLIR loop emitter became default June 2024 (TF PR #69775, flag --xla_gpu_mlir_emitter_level); openxla.org/xla/emitters documents that it 'traverses output elements linearly to guarantee coalesced writes' with dedicated vectorization passes — plausibly fixing the 4-elements-per-thread over-fetch generically, replacing the fragile cos(x*0) trigger hack and possibly the float64 loop_multiply_fusion_3 (571-586 us at 66% peak, no trigger applied). (2) The C2R forced input copy (jax#9946 'Force an input buffer copy...') and the post-inverse DoBlasScal are still in current XLA main (fft_thunk.cc) — upgrading does NOT deliver Part X item 6. (3) JAX 0.10.0-0.11.1 is a hazard window: IRFFT was lowered decomposed (~1.7x slower); 0.11.2 restored single C2R with Hermitian-symmetrization of the DC/Nyquist slices (commit 2fe0e2b; ~1.4x back, L40S 7.29->5.25 ms). (4) jax.ffi stable since 0.7.0 — the enabler for the cuFFT-LTO-callback track without maintaining a jaxlib fork. (5) Compatibility cost: jax >= 0.4.31 needs cudnn>=9; 0.11.2 needs cuDNN >= 9.10.2; torch 2.3.1 wheels pin nvidia-cudnn-cu12==8.9.2.26 — both-crash reported whichever cudnn wins (axlearn#858, jax discussion #21786). So the upgrade only works in a solver-only side env (the Part IX 'decouple' arm) or with a torch >= 2.4 upgrade (which changes ML numerics and needs its own gates). Zeroth step, free: probe whether jaxlib 0.4.28's bundled XLA already accepts --xla_gpu_mlir_emitter_level.

findings.what: vmap the step over a leading batch of 2 states; lax.fft natively batches leading dimensions, so every cuFFT call doubles its batch. The only kernels with idle-resource headroom are the three half-plane column passes (ncu: 4.2-wave tail): batch 2 gives 8.4 -> 9 waves, cutting tail waste from ~(5-4.2)/5 = 16% to (9-8.4)/9 = 6.7% of those kernels. All memory-bound fusions, row passes, products scale linearly (no efficiency change at 84-88% of peak). Frames for both trajectories come out bit-for-bit per-trajectory only if cuFFT picks the same kernels at batch 2 (not guaranteed).

dead_ends.idea: (d) Replace the full-plane 4096^2 C2C for (u - i v) by half-plane work (lean64-style packing of the u and v inverses into one half-size C2C)
dead_ends.why_not: Information-theoretically blocked: w = u_hat + i v_hat on the half-plane does not determine its own negative-ky half — w(-k) = conj(u_hat(k) - i v_hat(k)) = conj(w2(k)), so a half-plane first pass needs BOTH w and w2 transformed (2 x 2049 columns ~ the one full-plane pass's 4096). Three real fields (u, v, q) are already at the theoretical minimum of 2 complex transforms (one C2C pair + theta's C2R). The reachable reduction on this op is XR-2's pruned first pass (-153 us) and the already-known Part X item 4 forward packing (-75 us).

dead_ends.idea: (a, inverse side) Explicit two-pass theta IRFFT (pruned ifft over kept kx columns + transpose + 1-D C2R)
dead_ends.why_not: Nets +3 us by the byte arithmetic (pad 54 + ky pass 62 + transpose+pad 102 + forced C2R input copy 99 + C2R 96 + thunk scal 93 = 506 vs 503 us): XLA's defensive copy and DoBlasScal are unconditional (jax#9946; fft_thunk.cc on main), and the extra materializations eat the 33% column-pass pruning. Independently calibrated by JAX itself: the 0.10.0 decomposed IRFFT lowering measured ~1.7x one C2R (commit 2fe0e2b).

dead_ends.idea: (c alone) Transpose so column passes become row passes, without compaction/pruning
dead_ends.why_not: A 67.1 MB c64 transpose costs ~99-130 us (134 MB at 1.0-1.35 TB/s) but the column->row efficiency gain is only ~84 us per pass (134 MB at 48% -> 85% of attainable). Only pays when fused with the slice to the 1366 kept columns (XR-2), which shrinks both the transpose and the pass.

dead_ends.idea: (e) Command buffers / CUDA graphs (newer XLA defaults or flags)
dead_ends.why_not: GPU is 99.4% busy (Part X nsys): total gap is ~19 us/step — the upper bound on any launch-overhead fix.

dead_ends.idea: jnp.fft.fft(axis=0) as a way to reach cuFFT's strided batched column transform directly
dead_ends.why_not: JAX moveaxis-transposes non-trailing axes before lax.fft and back after (jax _src/numpy/fft.py) — the strided call is unreachable; you always pay two materialized transposes unless you manage layout yourself (XR-2).

dead_ends.idea: Upgrade landing on jax 0.10.0-0.11.1
dead_ends.why_not: That window lowers multi-dimensional IRFFT decomposed (~1.7x the single C2R, per commit 2fe0e2b) — a direct regression on our 503 us op; go straight to 0.11.2+.

dead_ends.idea: Newer cuFFT via the upgraded wheels as a standalone lever
dead_ends.why_not: Already measured a no-op: cuFFT 11.4.1 (CUDA 12.9.1) moved the FFT micro-table < 1% and lean32 by +0.06% (Part X); the column-pass inefficiency is in cuFFT's kernel choice, unchanged across these versions.

dead_ends.idea: Skipping the C2R normalization (1/N^2 scal) or input copy from inside XLA (donation, dead-temp inputs)
dead_ends.why_not: Both live in the FFT lowering/thunk, not in buffer assignment: the copy is forced (jax#9946 fix is unconditional) and DoBlasScal runs for every inverse type on current main — Part X item 6 stands; this needs the custom-call track. (The per-axis 1/4096 of an explicit ifft CAN be folded exactly into the products as a power-of-two multiply, used in XR-2.)

dead_ends.idea: Tensor-core FFTs (tcFFT, FlashFFTConv/Monarch, TurboFFT, error-corrected FP16/TF32 FFTs) for the 4096^2 transforms
dead_ends.why_not: The step is bandwidth-bound (ideal 2,819 MB/step = 2.09 ms at 1.35 TB/s; FFT passes already 78-88% of peak except the column passes), so tensor-core FLOP throughput buys nothing — bytes, not FLOPs, are the wall. Accuracy-wise: tcFFT is half-precision only (1.29-3.24x over cuFFT FP16 2-D; on A100 only 1.24x avg and 96-100% of cuFFT in bandwidth-bound cases — arXiv 2104.11471); the error-corrected mixed-precision 2-D FFT (Sorna et al., ICL/UTK 2018) costs ~2.5x the time of cuFFT FP32 for ~1e-4 error; Ootomo-Yokota 3xTF32 recovery targets GEMM, and NVIDIA's production TF32x3 example (MLIP blog, 2026) gives 1.5x only on compute-bound kernels; TurboFFT (arXiv 2405.02520/2412.05824) is a fault-tolerance design at 7-15% OVERHEAD vs cuFFT. No 2023-2026 result shows a tensor-core FFT beating cuFFT FP32 at FP32-level accuracy on a bandwidth-bound 4096^2 workload.

dead_ends.idea: Four-step / explicitly transposed batched 1-D FFTs to make the column pass coalesced
dead_ends.why_not: Arithmetic kills it: each explicit transpose is a full extra read+write of the array (134 MB for a 4096^2 complex64 plane = +99 us minimum at 1.35 TB/s, two transposes per transform ~ +0.2 ms), while the recoverable column-pass inefficiency is only ~0.09-0.13 ms per transform. Empirically, an NVIDIA forum case found a corrected batched-1-D Y-pass ~30% slower than cuFFT's built-in 2-D plan, and NVIDIA docs recommend contiguous datasets over manual decomposition. Only viable if the transpose fuses into an adjacent pointwise op AND the row FFT runs >85% of peak — which is FFT-3 (cuFFTDx) by another name.

dead_ends.idea: pyvkfft called from JAX via DLPack/CuPy as the production path for VkFFT
dead_ends.why_not: pyvkfft's backends are CuPy/PyCUDA/PyOpenCL only; its README mentions no DLPack or JAX interop. Crossing JAX jit <-> CuPy each solver step forces synchronization/copies that dwarf the ~0.1-0.3 ms at stake. Fine as an OFFLINE micro-benchmark of zero-padding (FFT-6's test plan), useless in the hot loop — the hot-loop route must be raw VkFFT behind the XLA FFI.

dead_ends.idea: Another cuFFT version bump (11.4.1+) or waiting for a faster base cuFFT
dead_ends.why_not: Already measured dead (Part X, job 7819082): cuFFT 11.4.1 from CUDA 12.9.1 moved the FFT micro-table <1% and lean32 by +0.06%; the slow column-pass kernels (regular_fft_factor at 41-52% of peak) are unchanged. CUDA 13.3's cuFFT changes are LTO-callback parity (useful for FFT-1), not faster sm_80 base kernels. Re-confirmed as not-a-lever; upgrading cuFFT matters only as a dependency of the callback route (needs >= 11.3 / CUDA 12.6u2).

findings.title: Integrating-factor (Lawson) AB3: weight the AB3 history by powers of the existing decay table; kills the measured first-order splitting error; opens dt toward the CFL limit
findings.what: Every surveyed GPU pseudo-spectral code integrates the linear (dissipation) term EXACTLY inside the stage/step structure, not as a separate first-order multiply after the explicit step: gTurbo2D (the Valadao/Boffetta group's single-GPU code that runs their SQG production, incl. arXiv 2504.07914) uses 'RK4EL' with omega_hat(t+dt) = exp(-L dt) * omega_hat(t) + ..., FourierFlows.jl ships ETDRK4 with cached contour-integral coefficients, pyspectral uses IF-RK4 (Lawson) 'with exact viscosity'. Our production step is the Lie split theta_{n+1} = E*(theta_n + inc) with E = exp(-(NU*kap^2 + MU*pos/kapi^2)*DT) (A-SQG_data.py lines 326-328) — already the exact exponential, but applied ONCE to all three AB3 history terms. IF-AB3 is theta_{n+1} = E*[theta_n + dt*(23/12 N_n - 16/12 E N_{n-1} + 5/12 E^2 N_{n-2})]: the only change is extra factors E and E^2 on the two older tendencies INSIDE the existing AB3 fusion, which already reads the decay table — E^2, E^3 are register math in a memory-bound kernel, so per-step cost is ~0. This removes the first-order split error that o1.2's dt ladder measured (D80/D30 ratio -1.42..-1.51, theory -1.50), restoring ~3rd-order overall accuracy, so dt can grow toward the CFL bound through the pre-set gates.

ETDRK4 with exact exp(L dt) and cached contour-integral coefficients (zeta, alpha, beta, Gamma over 32 circle points); their plain AB3 adds L explicitly (addlinearterm!) — strictly worse than our exact-exponential split; AB3 update line matches our 23/12,-16/12,5/12
'Integrating-factor RK4 (Lawson) with exact viscosity, CFL-adaptive dt'; the IF factorises into a table read, i.e. zero marginal cost
decay = ... * jnp.exp(-(NU*kap**2 + MU*pos/kapi**2)*DT) (lines 326-328): E is already the exact exponential and already read by the AB3 fusion — IF-AB3 is a coefficient-only change

findings.what: The code behind Part VII's pyspectral entry is public: github.com/walidhemati/pyspectral. The fastest variant (backends/cupy_cuda.py, kernels in src/pyspectral/kernels/spectral.cu via NVRTC) runs each stage as exactly: one fused physical-space product kernel -> one batched IN-PLACE R2C cuFFT -> one fused spectral kernel that assembles the nonlinear term, applies dealiasing and projection, performs the IF-RK4 update, and WRITES THE NEXT STAGE'S FFT INPUTS directly; 'no temporaries are allocated'; the integrating factor is read from a tiny 1-D table; a fused-inplace-graph variant replays one step as a CUDA graph. findings.what: Every surveyed fast code batches same-shape transforms into one plan (pyspectral: 'batched in-place R2C'; gTurbo2D batches its 5 FFTs/stage). findings.title: Native 16-bit (fp16/bf16) cuFFT transforms for the nonlinear term, state kept compensated-f32
findings.what: cuFFT natively supports fp16 and bf16 transforms through the cufftXt extensible-plan API (executiontype CUDA_C_16F / CUDA_C_16BF). Limitations fit us: power-of-two sizes only (4096 qualifies; for R2C/C2R 'size' = real elements), SM_53+/SM_80+ (A100 OK for both), single GPU, no strides on the real side (our arrays are contiguous). bf16 execution internally mixes f32 and bf16 arithmetic. The step would keep the hi+lo compensated float32 state and AB3 update exactly as in lean32ek_fast, and run only the 5 transforms (and optionally the physical-space products/build_w) in 16-bit. fp16 needs range handling: an un-normalized forward 4096^2 FFT concentrates up to ~N^2*O(1) ~ 1.7e7 in low-k coefficients, far above fp16 max 65504, so a fixed power-of-two prescale (1/N per dimension, exact) must be folded in -- exactly the fixed-shift block-floating-point schedule of arXiv 2605.28451, which got a 4096-point FP16 FFT pipeline within 0.1 dB of the FP32 reference at 42 dB SQNR (on Apple M1, 2.2x vs FP32). bf16 has f32 range (no overflow) but only 8 mantissa bits. Route: NOT reachable via jnp.fft (JAX FFT is f32/f64 only); reachable via CuPy's experimental cupy.cuda.cufft.XtPlanNd (documented; a preliminary CuPy test measured fp16 FFT ~2x faster than f32), via nvmath-python (device-API FFT lists numpy.float16 among supported compute precisions; host API adds LTO prolog/epilog callbacks, cuFFT >= 11.3 / CUDA 12.6u2, numba-cuda >= 0.27), or via a custom XLA FFI call so it stays inside the jitted step. A lower-risk variant: keep f32 execution and use LTO load/store callbacks only to convert HBM storage of FFT inputs/outputs to 16-bit -- but that halves only the outer load/store, not the inter-pass intermediate, so it saves only ~25% of FFT bytes. Weather-model precedent that 16-bit spectral transforms need not harm the physics (with rescaling and low modes kept in higher precision): Hatfield et al. PASC 2019 on IFS Legendre transforms (up to 2.5x on that kernel).

findings.title: Stochastic rounding of the state update instead of the compensated hi+lo pair
findings.what: Part XI showed plain-f32 state update is biased because sub-ulp per-step increments round deterministically (31% delta error in the 1-mode emulation), and the compensated hi+lo update fixes it (8.8e-8) at a measured cost of +0.138 ms/step (2.698 measured vs 3.21-0.557-0.093 = 2.560 implied without hi/lo). The weather/climate literature established that stochastic rounding removes exactly this class of error in expectation: Paxton, Chantry, Klöwer, Saffin & Palmer (J. Climate 2022) show Float16 stagnation/systematic rounding error is 'successfully mitigated by stochastic rounding', with Float16sr error small relative to high-precision variability, and Klöwer et al. 2020 document the stalling mechanism for deterministic 16-bit rounding. Here SR would be applied at f32 (ulp 6e-8), replacing the lo array entirely: round theta_hi + inc stochastically using per-element random bits generated inside the AB3 fusion (counter-based, deterministic per step index and mode, so runs stay reproducible). NVIDIA GPUs expose no hardware SR for floating-point adds (we found none in CUDA docs; SR hardware exists on Graphcore-class chips), so this is a software bit-twiddle + threefry-style hash in the fusion — extra compute in a kernel that is bandwidth-bound at ~89% of DRAM peak, so some compute slack exists but the cost must be measured.

findings.title: Co-scheduling the ML step and solver (streams/MPS/green contexts/MIG): the remaining headroom is ~3%, and the mechanism explains why
findings.what: Ceiling arithmetic: per optimizer step the solver runs 480 x 2.698 ms = 1.295 s and the ML step 0.40 s; perfect overlap saves 0.40/1.695 = 23.6% of wall. The thread-overlap experiment already hides <= 21%, so every co-scheduling mechanism combined can add at most ~3% more. The literature explains why nothing fancier helps: green contexts (CUDA 12.4 driver API; runtime API since CUDA 13.1, plus static SM partitioning for MPS on Ampere+) partition SMs only — NVIDIA's own docs state DRAM bandwidth and L2 remain shared, and concurrency is not guaranteed; MPS likewise shares the memory hierarchy; only MIG physically partitions bandwidth (GPC granularity on A100), but a bandwidth-bound solver in a MIG slice just runs proportionally slower, conserving GPU-seconds. Measured colocation interference (SoCC'25 ETH study) shows up to 2.15x slowdown when combined working sets exceed L2 — consistent with the solver (99.4% busy, bandwidth-bound) leaving almost nothing for a co-resident memory-bound ML step beyond its compute-bound fraction. This effectively closes track (c)'s co-scheduling question: the 21% already achieved is near the ceiling, and the real win was the already-measured decoupling (equal GPU-seconds, 3.8x shorter steps).

dead_ends.idea: DFT-as-GEMM on A100 FP64 tensor cores (DMMA via cuBLAS) for the transform passes
dead_ends.why_not: Arithmetic kills it: one 4096^2 c128 2D transform as matrix multiplies = 2 dims x 4096^3 complex MACs x 8 flops = 1.10e12 flops; at the A100's 19.5 TFLOPS FP64-TC peak that is >= 56 ms, vs the measured 1.2 ms cuFFT c128 C2C (micro-table, Part VIII). O(N^3) GEMM cannot beat O(N^2 log N) memory-bound FFT at N=4096; the GEMM-spectral wins in the literature (ECMWF ecTrans, Hatfield) are for Legendre transforms, which are inherently matrix products.

dead_ends.idea: Ozaki-scheme FP64 emulation on INT8/FP8 tensor cores (ozIMMU, Ozaki-II/GEMMul8, cuBLAS CUBLAS_COMPUTE_64F_EMULATED) for the solver
dead_ends.why_not: It accelerates GEMMs only, and our FFT is memory-bound — compute is not the bottleneck anywhere in the step (all ops 41-88% of DRAM peak). Emulation multiplies the GEMM count (ozIMMU 3-18 INT8 slices; Ozaki-I ~s(s+1)/2 inner GEMMs), so even the DFT-as-GEMM route above gets no cheaper in time. NVIDIA's productized FP64 emulation (cuBLAS, CUDA 12.9/13.0u2, 1.5-3x on ecTrans/BerkeleyGW) is Blackwell-only — not available on Polaris A100s at all.

dead_ends.idea: fp16x2 / error-free-transformation split FFTs (Markidis, Ootomo-Yokota style) to get f32 accuracy from 16-bit hardware
dead_ends.why_not: The hi+lo split doubles the array count, so HBM bytes equal plain f32 — and our FFTs are bandwidth-bound, so the time returns to f32 time. The technique's wins (51 TFLOPS on A100 FP16 TCs vs 19.5 FP32 peak) are compute-throughput wins, irrelevant when the kernels sit at 41-88% of DRAM peak. Only pure 16-bit storage (FR1) halves bytes.

dead_ends.idea: Temporal blocking / fusing several AB3 time steps on chip (FlashFFTStencil/StencilFFT-style multi-step fusion)
dead_ends.why_not: FFT-based multi-timestep fusion works by raising the transformed LINEAR kernel to the number of steps; SQG's advection is nonlinear, requiring physical-space products (u*theta, v*theta) every single step, so the step chain cannot be collapsed. Classic stencil temporal blocking needs locality; a global 4096^2 FFT touches all 67 MB per field per pass, far beyond SM-local storage, so no inter-step on-chip reuse exists. The only 'linear substep' (damping) is already a fused table multiply.

dead_ends.idea: Spectral deferred correction / parallel-in-time (pySDC GPU, diagonal SDC) to take bigger effective steps
dead_ends.why_not: On one GPU, SDC with M collocation nodes costs ~M-1 tendency evaluations (= full FFT sets) per sweep per step, vs AB3's one; dt headroom is CFL-capped at ~1.9x (CFL 0.374 vs ~0.72 limit) and is already being harvested for free by the gated larger-dt arms (30/32 steps/frame PASS noise + bias magnitude), so SDC's extra FFTs can never pay back on a memory-bound step. Parallel-in-time buys wall-clock only with more GPUs at efficiency <= 0.81 (pySDC Rayleigh-Benard, arXiv 2610.17942), i.e. worse GPU-seconds — dominated by the already-measured decoupling (equal GPU-seconds, 3.8x shorter steps). Changing the integrator would also re-open the first-order splitting question through the full gate battery for at best zero net gain.

dead_ends.idea: Learned / ML-accelerated solver steps (neural surrogates, learned correction of coarse steps)
dead_ends.why_not: science change — the solver's output distribution would be a model artifact, exactly what the training data must not contain.

dead_ends.idea: MIG partitioning to co-run solver and ML step with bandwidth isolation
dead_ends.why_not: MIG is the only mechanism that partitions DRAM bandwidth (GPC granularity on A100), but partitioning conserves total bandwidth: the bandwidth-bound solver in a slice slows proportionally, and the frame->training dependence is sequential, so there is no throughput reshaping to exploit. See FR4: residual co-scheduling headroom <= ~3% by ceiling arithmetic.

dead_ends.idea: Scale-selective precision (Düben/Hatfield: low-k modes in high precision, high-k in 16-bit) applied inside the transforms
dead_ends.why_not: The FFT mixes all scales within a pass, so per-scale precision cannot be assigned inside a single cuFFT transform; it only applies to coefficient STORAGE, and our state must stay compensated-f32 anyway for the Part XI bias mechanism. The storage-only version collapses into FR1's callback-storage variant.

Hatfield PDF read IN FULL (13 slides): it is a 2021 ECMWF 'Single and half Precision in Earth-System Models' deck, not PASC 2019 itself (it cites Hatfield et al. 2019, doi 10.1145/3324989.3325711); the up-to-2.5x is half-vs-SINGLE per-GEMM Legendre speed on Fugaku A64FX (LEDIR 2.48-2.49x, LEINV 1.29-1.86x, 'transposing kills the speed-up'), and the no-skill-harm result is the 2019 software-emulation study with rescaling — the precedent holds but is CPU/emulation, not GPU-measured. nvmath-python: the cited 1.0.0 page exists but is truncated; a search of the current docs confirms numba-cuda >= 0.27 for compile_prolog/epilog, cuFFT 11.3 / CUDA 12.6U2 for LTO callbacks, device-API (cuFFTDx) precision list includes numpy.float16, bf16 not listed — all as claimed; NEW detail: the callback compile helpers accept element dtypes [f32, f64, c64, c128] only, so the 16-bit-storage-callback variant needs hand-written numba loads, not the stock helper.
verdicts.gain_check: Arithmetic verified against Part X: 615+540+503 = 1,658 us FFT family, halved ~0.83 ms; products+build_w 253+235 = 488 -> ~0.24 ms; net 2.698 -> ~1.7-1.9 ms checks out as a FIRST-ORDER UPPER BOUND. Caveat the finding understates: ~40% of FFT time is the column passes at 41-52% of DRAM peak, limited by uncoalesced sectors / shared-memory bank conflicts (Part X ncu), not purely by bytes — halving element size need not halve those kernels, so the realistic saving is likely below 0.83 ms. No double count with trigger/ring: the per-op FFT numbers are unchanged between lean32 and lean32ek_fast. Storage-callback variant's 25%-of-FFT-bytes (~0.41 ms bound, claimed 0.3-0.4) is correct (outer load+store = 2 of 4 array traversals per 2-pass transform).
verdicts.applicability_check: A100 qualifies (SM_80 >= SM_75/SM_80); 4096 power-of-two qualifies; contiguous arrays OK. Physics unchanged in the state/AB3 (gated statistical change in the tendency, correctly declared). TWO wrinkles: (1) 'custom XLA FFI call so it stays inside the jitted step' is NOT available on our jax 0.4.28 — jax.extend.ffi.ffi_call soft-launched in 0.4.31 (FFI headers packaged from 0.4.29; JAX changelog/PR #23478), so the in-jit route needs a jax/jaxlib upgrade or the legacy custom_call API; CuPy/nvmath otherwise sit outside jit with dlpack boundary crossings per step. (2) LTO-callback variants need cuFFT >= 11.3 (CUDA 12.6U2) — Part X phase 3 showed a pip cuFFT 11.4.1 can be loaded, so reachable. Bias risk correctly flagged: per-mode deterministic 16-bit tendency rounding is the structure gate B detects, and lean32ek's margin was only ~100x. Novelty 'new' holds: Part VII covered callbacks/packing/implicit dealiasing, not 16-bit execution.
verdicts.corrections: (a) fp16 minimum arch is SM_75 per current cuFFT docs, not SM_53. (b) Hatfield evidence: 2021 ECMWF slide deck (now read in full) citing the PASC 2019 emulation paper; 2.48-2.49x is half-vs-single GEMM on Fugaku A64FX, CPU not GPU. (c) The 0.83 ms FFT saving is an upper bound — the column passes (857 us of the 1,658) are coalescing/bank-conflict-limited at 41-52% of peak, not byte-limited. (d) The in-jit route requires jax >= 0.4.31 (XLA FFI) or legacy custom_call; we run 0.4.28. (e) nvmath's callback compile helpers do not accept fp16 element dtypes. Core proposal and test plan otherwise stand; phase-1 micro-benchmark remains the right go/no-go.

verdicts.source_check: Paxton et al. 2022: the AMS URL returns 403 (bot-blocked) but the paper is real and says what is claimed (J. Climate 35, 1215-1229, doi 10.1175/JCLI-D-21-0343.1; open copies on arXiv 2104.15076 / White Rose) — SR mitigates stagnation from deterministic rounding at low precision. Klöwer 2020 JAMES URL also 403; not independently re-read. The sources are fine; the finding fails on the repo, not the literature.
verdicts.gain_check: REFUTED BY EXISTING MEASUREMENTS THE TRACK MISSED. (1) The hi/lo cost arithmetic uses an implied 2.560 ms (3.21-0.557-0.093), but Part X MEASURED lean32_u1_ring3 at 2.524 ms, so the compensation's fast-path cost is 2.698-2.524 = 0.174 ms, not 0.138. (2) An SR variant already exists and was timed in job 7824121: lean32sr = lean32e with the state stochastically rounded, jax.random.bits(fold_in(key, tc)) counter-based per (step, component) — exactly the proposed design — at 2.793 ms/step, i.e. 0.095 ms SLOWER than lean32ek_fast (2.698), though it lacks the u1 trigger and 3-slot ring (taxonomy.py builds it with make_call defaults u1=False, ring=2), so an SR+trigger+ring variant is untimed and could plausibly land near ~2.2 ms. (3) Accuracy: Part XII measured lean32sr e_Delta = 1.43e-5 overall vs lean32ek's 9.43e-6, and 5.84e-5 vs 1.91e-5 at k 1-2 — SR is WORSE than the compensated state at o1.2's lag (the added ulp variance), and it shows a likely REAL d-aligned bias term B_d ~ -1e-7 to -9e-7 (z_d -4.6 at k 8-16, -5.5 at k 16-32, negative in 6 of 8 bands) shared with lean32ek and attributed (as a hypothesis) to the float32 tendency they share — SR does not remove the learnable-bias question, because the remaining bias is not the state-update mechanism SR fixes.
verdicts.applicability_check: Technique applies and is already applied; reproducibility design (counter-based bits) already solved in lean32_fast.py. Novelty 'new' is wrong: lean32_fast.py's docstring cites Paxton 2022 and Kimpson et al. 2023 QJRMS for exactly this, 'checked against Crossref 2026-11-10', and lean32sr ran as negative control 2 in the Part XII taxonomy. The proposed test plan's phase (a) (rerun the 1-mode emulation with SR) and phase (c) (delta gates) are partially moot — the full-solver bias/noise characterization already exists on 16 archived states.
verdicts.corrections: Corrected statement: stochastic rounding is already implemented (SQG/analysis/opt/taxonomy/lean32_fast.py, mode='sr') and measured (job 7824121): 2.793 ms without the trigger/ring fixes, e_Delta 1.43e-5 (1.5x worse than lean32ek overall, 3x worse at k 1-2), with a suspected real d-aligned bias of its own. The only live remnant of FR3 is a small, untested speed question: build lean32sr with u1=True, ring=3 (one-line change) and time it — if it lands ~0.3-0.5 ms under lean32ek_fast AND the user accepts SR's higher variance and its unresolved d-term, it could displace the hi/lo state; expected net is modest and the accuracy direction is adverse.

verdicts.source_check: CUDA Programming Guide green-contexts page re-opened: SM/work-queue partitioning, 'concurrent execution ... is not guaranteed', CUDA 13.1 runtime-API contexts and MPS static partitioning all confirmed; but the page does NOT say DRAM bandwidth and L2 remain shared. NVIDIA blog re-opened: it also does NOT contain the claimed bandwidth/L2/MIG statements — the finding's attribution 'NVIDIA's own docs state' is wrong. The substance is instead in the cited ETH paper, read in full (Elvinger, Strati, Enright Jerger, Klimovic, 'Understanding GPU Resource Interference One Level Deeper', SoCC '25, doi 10.1145/3772052.3772270): 'At 16MB, slowdown peaks at 2.15x due to the combined 64MB working set exceeding L2 capacity' (two copy kernels, H100, green contexts) and §5.2 'CUDA green contexts ... only partition SMs and not DRAM channels' — 2.15x and the SM-only-partition mechanism confirmed, from the right primary source.
verdicts.gain_check: THE CEILING ARITHMETIC IS WRONG. Part III B (notes lines 239-278) defines the 21%: overlap efficiency = (solver_only + ml_only - combined)/min(...) = 0.209, i.e. thread_fixed 'hides only 21% OF THE ML STEP' — not 21 percentage points of wall. At the measured (ref-solver) speeds that is ~0.21 x 0.417 s ~ 0.088 s of a 4.887 s optimizer step = ~1.8% of wall. The 23.6% ceiling (0.40/1.695 at lean32ek_fast speed) is a wall fraction. So the measured overlap is ~9% of the ceiling, not ~89%, and the residual co-scheduling headroom is up to ~22% of wall, not <= ~3%. The 'closes track (c)' conclusion does not follow from arithmetic. What survives is the mechanism argument: the solver alone keeps the GPU 99.2-99.6% busy and is DRAM-bound, the ML step's GPU time stretched 4.6x (416 -> 1,910 ms) under colocation, and SM-partitioning tools cannot partition the contended resource — so large additional overlap is unlikely, but that is now an inference, not a measured closure; also the 21% was measured with the 9.3 ms ref solver, never with the 3.44x faster candidate, where the solver:ML ratio (1.295:0.40) and the efficiency could differ.
verdicts.applicability_check: Correct that CUDA 13.1 runtime green contexts postdate our stack and that MPS needs process separation + IPC. MIG/bandwidth-conservation reasoning is sound. Bitwise exactness claim (scheduling only) is fine. Not already in Part VII/X beyond the raw 21% measurement, so 'deepens' is fair — but it deepens with a misread.
verdicts.corrections: (a) Replace the ceiling claim: measured overlap = 21% of the ML step ~ 1.8% of wall (ref solver); theoretical ceiling = 23.6% of wall (fast solver); residual headroom up to ~22% of wall, NOT <= 3%. (b) Re-attribute the bandwidth/L2-shared statement to the SoCC '25 paper §5.2 (green contexts 'only partition SMs and not DRAM channels'); NVIDIA's doc and blog do not say it. (c) The recommendation to prefer the already-measured decoupling (equal GPU-seconds, 3.8x shorter steps) still stands on the mechanism evidence, and the proposed cheap streams/MPS experiment — run with the FAST solver — is now worth more than the finding itself suggests, since it would test a ~22%-of-wall headroom, not a 3% one.

The FlashFFTStencil dead-end reasoning is sound: FFT-based temporal fusion needs a linear constant-coefficient kernel raised to a power; SQG's advection requires physical-space products every step. The recommendation to read 2605.28451 in full before any FR1 build is right (only its abstract was read; the exact shift schedule and its NVIDIA transferability are unverified — it is an Apple-Silicon/AMX paper).
